newsitem.title: UK: LME - Metal markets braced for change in wake of scandal.
newsitem.headline: LME - Metal markets braced for change in wake of scandal.

text.p: The winds of change are set to blow through the metals trading world over the coming months in the wake of the Sumitomo copper storm.

Senior industry sources said there could be important alterations to trading on the London Metal Exchange (LME), the hub of world industrial metals trading, although the market would not change beyond recognition.
"I am sure there will be quite a lot of changes to the way the LME works and monitors the markets," said one.
The shape of the metals market to come will be one of the hot topics of discussion at next week's LME Week in London, annual shindig for the metals industry worldwide.
In June Japan's Sumitomo Corp announced it had run up losses now estimated at $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading by its eclipsed star trader Yasuo Hamanaka.

The announcement sent copper prices crashing, plunged some LME members' books into the red, prevented traders from collecting bonuses and sparked more regulatory probes into the murky world of base metals dealing. It also seriously undermined confidence in the LME as a price reference point for the metals industry.

In response the LME called on top UK financial watchdog the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) to carry out a broad review of the metal markets, which may provide the basis for some of the changes that are made.
The most important changes many users feel are necessary are also the most contentious - increasing transparency and the LME's regulatory powers.
The problem with both issues is that a large part of base metals trade worldwide is carried out through over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, which do not come under the LME's control.
And some of the biggest metal traders, including Sumitomo, are not LME members but trade through other parties.
"To the extent that the OTC markets are probably outside of the UK and the jurisdiction of the LME it's hard to see how you can improve visibility of what's going on," said one source.
And as well as the practical difficulties, there is also strong resistance from some sides of the industry to giving away too much information about people's positions.
But information on daily volumes and open interest could be a way of making the LME less opaque, a trader said.
The LME has already taken the step of introducing its own average rate (Asian) option contract from the start of 1997, bringing a large part of OTC options business under its control.

Concrete proposals understood to be under discussion are lengthening open outcry trading sessions, trading options on the market floor as well as futures, and bringing more people on to the board of directors from outside the metals industry.
Quite apart from changes to the trading framework, many dealers are convinced that the LME faces the added challenge of members downsizing operations in response to falling volumes.
As a result the high level of job insecurity among traders may continue, particularly in the beleaguered options sector.
But further ahead business may eventually recover, giving an incentive to ride out the Sumitomo shake-out.
"Those who can ride out the storm will be in a strong position in a few years' time," a trader said.
